questions.question: In an AC generator, at which position of the rotating coil is the induced emf maximum?
options: When the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field
When the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the magnetic field
When the flux linked with the coil is maximum
When the plane of the coil makes $45^\circ$ with the magnetic field

solution.key_concept: The emf depends on the rate of change of flux, not on the flux itself.
steps: Flux $\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t$ gives emf $\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$.
The emf is maximum when the flux is zero, that is, when the coil plane is parallel to B.
At this position the flux is zero but changing fastest.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): When the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field
solution.why_not_others: When the plane is perpendicular to B, the flux is maximum and the emf is zero. Options 2 and 3 describe the same zero-emf position. At $45^\circ$ the emf is only $\varepsilon_0/\sqrt{2}$.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that maximum flux gives maximum emf.
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember the pairing: flux maximum means emf zero, and flux zero means emf maximum.

questions.question: A coil of 100 turns and area $0.02\ \text{m}^2$ rotates at 50 revolutions per second in a uniform magnetic field of $0.5$ T. What is the peak emf induced? (Take $\pi = 3.14$)

solution.key_concept: Peak emf is $\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega$ with $\omega = 2\pi f$.
steps: $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi \times 50 = 100\pi$ rad/s.
$\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega = 100 \times 0.5 \times 0.02 \times 100\pi$.
$\varepsilon_0 = 100\pi \approx 314$ V.
solution.why_not_others: 50 V results from using f instead of $\omega$. 222 V is the rms value, not the peak value. 3.14 V results from leaving out N.
solution.common_trap: Substituting the frequency f directly in place of $\omega$.
solution.time_saving_tip: First compute $NBA = 1$ Wb; the peak emf is then simply $\omega = 100\pi$.

questions.question: An AC generator produces a peak emf $\varepsilon_0$ at frequency f. The angular speed of its coil is doubled and the magnetic field is halved. What are the new peak emf and frequency?

solution.key_concept: Peak emf is $\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega$, and the frequency of the emf equals the rotation frequency.
steps: New peak emf is $NA(B/2)(2\omega) = NBA\omega = \varepsilon_0$.
The frequency depends only on $\omega$, so doubling $\omega$ doubles it to $2f$.
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 ignores the change in frequency. Option 3 ignores the halving of B. Option 4 halves the emf and keeps f unchanged, which ignores the doubling of $\omega$.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that the frequency also depends on B, or that an unchanged peak emf means an unchanged frequency.
solution.time_saving_tip: Track the two quantities separately: the emf goes as $B\omega$, while the frequency goes as $\omega$ alone.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Doubling the angular speed of the coil of an AC generator doubles the peak emf.
statements.R: The frequency of the emf produced by an AC generator equals the frequency of rotation of its coil.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Peak emf $\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega$ is proportional to $\omega$; the frequency of the emf is a separate result.
steps: Since $\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega$, doubling $\omega$ doubles the peak emf, so A is true.
Since $\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$, the emf has the rotation frequency, so R is true.
A is explained by $\varepsilon_0 \propto \omega$ (the flux changes faster), not by the frequency relation.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: R describes the frequency, not the amplitude, so it cannot explain A. Both statements are true, so options 3 and 4 are wrong.
solution.common_trap: Linking the two statements because both involve $\omega$.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: In an AC generator, the induced emf is zero at the instant the flux linked with the coil is maximum.
statements.II: For a generator with $\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$, at an instant when the emf equals half its peak value, the magnitude of the flux linked with the coil is $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}NBA$.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: The flux $\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t$ and the emf $\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$ are $90^\circ$ out of phase.
steps: When the flux is maximum, $\cos\omega t = \pm 1$, so $\sin\omega t = 0$ and the emf is zero. Statement I is correct.
If $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0/2$, then $\sin\omega t = 1/2$ and $|\cos\omega t| = \sqrt{3}/2$.
So $|\Phi| = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}NBA$. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
solution.why_not_others: Both statements follow directly from the phase relation, so options 2, 3 and 4 are wrong.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that half the peak emf means half the maximum flux.
solution.time_saving_tip: Use $\sin^2\omega t + \cos^2\omega t = 1$ to relate the emf fraction to the flux fraction.

questions.question: Which of the following quantities is the same in the primary and secondary of an ideal step-up transformer?

solution.key_concept: A transformer changes voltage and current but does not change frequency or power.
steps: In a step-up transformer, the voltage increases and the current decreases.
The number of turns differs, with $N_s > N_p$.
The frequency stays unchanged.
solution.why_not_others: Voltage increases and current decreases in a step-up transformer. The turns differ by definition.
solution.common_trap: Thinking a transformer can change the frequency of the AC supply.

questions.question: A transformer of efficiency 80% steps down 220 V to 11 V. The secondary delivers a current of 4 A. What is the current in the primary?

steps: Output power $= 11 \times 4 = 44$ W.
Input power $= 44/0.8 = 55$ W.
Primary current $I_p = 55/220 = 0.25$ A.
solution.why_not_others: 0.2 A assumes an ideal transformer. 0.16 A multiplies by $\eta$ instead of dividing by it. 80 A inverts the current ratio.
solution.common_trap: Multiplying the output power by the efficiency instead of dividing by it.
solution.time_saving_tip: Input power is always greater than output power in a real transformer, so $I_p$ must exceed the ideal value of 0.2 A.

questions.question: A power of 100 kW is transmitted through lines of total resistance $5\ \Omega$. The transmission voltage is raised from 10 kV to 20 kV while the transmitted power is kept the same. What is the new power loss in the lines?

solution.key_concept: Line loss is $P_{loss} = I^2R$ with $I = P/V$, so the loss varies as $1/V^2$.
steps: At 10 kV, $I = 10^5/10^4 = 10$ A, so the loss is $10^2 \times 5 = 500$ W.
New loss $= 5^2 \times 5 = 125$ W.
solution.why_not_others: 250 W assumes the loss varies as $1/V$. 1000 W assumes the loss increases in proportion to V. 2000 W assumes the loss increases as $V^2$.
solution.common_trap: Using $V^2/R$ with the transmission voltage instead of $I^2R$ with the line current.
solution.time_saving_tip: Doubling the voltage cuts the loss to one-fourth: $500/4 = 125$ W.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_II.label: III
list_II.text: Soft-iron core with a narrow hysteresis loop

list_II.label: IV
list_II.text: Winding the coils one over the other

solution.key_concept: Each energy loss in a real transformer has its own remedy.
steps: Flux leakage is reduced by winding the coils one over the other: A-IV.
Copper loss is reduced by using thick wires: B-II.
Eddy-current loss is reduced by a laminated core: C-I.
Hysteresis loss is reduced by a soft-iron core with a narrow loop: D-III.
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 swaps the remedies for flux leakage and copper loss. Option 3 swaps the remedies for eddy-current and hysteresis losses. Option 4 assigns the laminated core to flux leakage.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the remedies for eddy-current loss and hysteresis loss, since both concern the core.
solution.time_saving_tip: Fix C-I first, because lamination is the standard remedy for eddy currents. Only options 1 and 2 keep C-I.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about transformers are correct?

statements.A: An ideal step-up transformer increases the voltage and decreases the current.
statements.B: A transformer can work on steady DC if its turns ratio is large enough.
statements.C: The frequency of the output voltage equals the frequency of the input voltage.
statements.D: An ideal step-up transformer increases the power by the factor $N_s/N_p$.
statements.E: Transmitting power at high voltage reduces $I^2R$ losses in the lines.

solution.key_concept: An ideal transformer conserves power and frequency, and it works only on AC through mutual induction.
steps: A is correct: since $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$, the current falls as the voltage rises.
B is incorrect: steady DC gives a constant flux, which induces no emf.
C is correct: the frequency is unchanged.
D is incorrect: an ideal transformer conserves power.
E is correct: high voltage means low current, so the $I^2R$ loss is smaller.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A, C and E only
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 leaves out the true statement E. Option 2 includes the false statement B. Option 4 includes the false statement D.
solution.common_trap: Believing a step-up transformer increases power along with voltage.
solution.time_saving_tip: Eliminate any option containing B or D; only option 3 has neither and also includes A, C and E.
